docs.title: Phase 5 & Phase 6 (Implemented): Thresholded Async Worker, Live Maps View Options & Documentation Sync
docs.text:
• Phase 5 (spectroview/viewmodel/vm_live_maps.py, spectroview/main.py):
  • ASYNC_SPECTRUM_THRESHOLD = 25_000 (configurable on VMLiveMaps(..., async_threshold=...)): batches below 25k active spectra remain synchronous; batches >= 25,000 dispatch to a dedicated QThreadPool(maxThreadCount=1) _LiveMapWorker (QRunnable) bridged via parented _LiveMapWorkerBridge(QObject).
  • Monotonic _generation_id + MapData.data_version verification discards superseded drag/clear frames safely, and shutdown() drains active workers on Main.closeEvent().
  • Verified by tests/unit/viewmodel/test_vm_live_maps_async.py.
  • Phase 6 (spectroview/view/components/v_live_maps.py, v_live_maps_legend_editor.py):
  • Added top-right [Show Legend | More view options] toolbar in VLiveMaps with client-side cached re-rendering (zero spectral recomputation): Linear/Log X, Y, and Color (Z) LogNorm scaling with non-positive domain fallbacks, Line / Dot / Line + Dots styles + line width & dot size, Show/Hide legend, legend location/columns/font size, draggable & double-click-editable canvas legends (LiveMapsLegendEditorDialog) synchronized with multi-1D header chips, Show grid, Share Y-axis (1D), Heatmap smoothing, Show colorbars, and Reset view options.
  • Synchronized docs/developer/maps.md, docs/developer/spectra.md, and docs/user_manual/spectra_maps.md.
  • Verified by expanded tests/unit/view/test_live_maps.py.

docs.title: A. Objective
docs.text: Keep the GUI responsive during heavy multi-map batches (total active spectra > 25,000 or massive 90,000+ single maps), and synchronize all SPECTROview documentation surfaces required by AGENTS.md.

docs.title: B. Files and Components
docs.text:
• spectroview/viewmodel/vm_live_maps.py (background QRunnable + QThreadPool + generation_id)
  • Documentation surfaces:
  • docs/developer/ (Maps Workspace, Live Maps & VMLiveMaps architecture)
  • docs/user_manual/ (Multi-map selection, Live Maps 1D multi-profile comparison, 2D Switcher, R/B Ratio) + refreshed Modern Dark screenshots in docs/user_manual_images/
  • docs/api/ (note if any public selection helper is exposed; existing spectroview/api/ signatures remain untouched)

docs.title: C. Technical Implementation
docs.text:
1. Thresholded QThreadPool Offload (vm_live_maps.py):
  2. Below 25,000 total active spectra across target maps: stay on synchronous timer-coalesced path (lowest overhead, deterministic).
  3. Above 25,000: spawn a lightweight QRunnable on a dedicated QThreadPool (maxThreadCount=1 or queued with self._generation_id += 1 cancellation):
    • On main thread before launching worker: snapshot references + slice inputs safely alongside gen = self._generation_id and data_versions.
    • Inside worker thread: run NumPy slice-first compute + cached Delaunay grid evaluation (pure NumPy/SciPy math, zero Qt widget calls).
    • Emit result signal through a QObject bridge parented cleanly to VMLiveMaps (obeying AGENTS.md PySide6 lifetime rules) -> main thread checks if gen != self._generation_id: return before populating _intensity_cache and emitting map_data_ready / multi_profile_data_ready.
  4. Thread Lifetime & Teardown Safety:
  5. Connect parent widget/app cleanup (destroyed / clear_workspace) to increment _generation_id, stop _timer, and avoid dangling worker callbacks writing to destroyed QObjects.
  6. Mandatory Documentation & Visual Asset Synchronization:
  7. Update User Manual, Developer Guide, and verify Public API stability guarantees. Capture Modern Dark UI visuals showing multi-map selection + Live Maps 1D multi-profile legend strip & 2D switcher (following native font rendering rules with no headless tofu boxes).

docs.title: D. Dependencies
docs.text: Requires Phases 0–4.

docs.title: E. Performance Considerations
docs.text: • Offloads ~180–500 ms NumPy compute on massive batches off the Qt UI thread so mouse/bracket dragging stays visually smooth while Matplotlib Agg draws run solely on the Qt main thread when results arrive.

docs.title: F. Edge Cases
docs.text:
• Workspace cleared or map deleted while worker is mid-compute -> bumped _generation_id drops stale worker output cleanly; worker holds sliced inputs safely.
  • Rapid bracket dragging fires new generation -> in-flight outdated generations are discarded cleanly upon completion without overwriting newer data.

docs.text:
• Large (90,000+) map calculations do not block mouse/UI events during compute phase; stale async frames never render.
  • All modified files pass pyflakes, full unit/integration test suite passes under QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen, and all doc surfaces match implementation.

docs.title: 7. Phase VI — Performance Validation & Benchmarking Strategy
A. Measurement Protocol
docs.text:
All performance checks execute headless under QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen with isolated QSettings and deterministic synthetic fixtures:

  • Timing: time.perf_counter() bracketing (1) pure compute (compute_spectral_parameter / VMLiveMaps._recalculate_batch), (2) full view draw (QApplication.processEvents() + Matplotlib canvas draw), and (3) end-to-end UI event \(\rightarrow\) canvas idle.
  • Memory: tracemalloc.start() measuring peak_alloc_mb per step so temporary float64 full-matrix regressions fail immediately.
  • Call/Redraw Hygiene: Lightweight signal/method counters verifying zero duplicate VMLiveMaps batch runs (1 batch per logical change) and 0 compute calls when Live Maps is hidden or when heatmap points are clicked.

docs.title: SPECTROview — Strategy A (Pure-Python, NumPy, SciPy & PySide6) Performance Audit & Optimization Roadmap
docs.text: Document Status: Re-Audited Under Controlled Idle-CPU Conditions, Empirically Benchmarked & Implementation-Ready Roadmap Target Architecture: Strategy A — Pure-Python Optimization (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, PySide6, Matplotlib) Decision Context: Following a full-repository technical audit and controlled re-profiling of SPECTROview (v26.48.2, 225 Python modules across model/, viewmodel/, view/, fit_engine/, api/, application/, and ai_agent/), Rust migration is not necessary. Over 85–90% of the achievable end-to-end performance and memory improvements can be captured purely in Python by fixing data-structure choices, memory layout (F_CONTIGUOUS vs C_CONTIGUOUS), OpenBLAS thread oversubscription, memory duplication, algorithmic complexity, and Qt widget virtualization—while preserving zero-compiler py3-none-any.whl packaging and cross-platform CI/CD simplicity.

docs.title: 1. Controlled Benchmarking Methodology & Why the Re-Audit Changed the Baseline
1.1 Controlled Test Environment
docs.text:
All baseline and prototype measurements in this document were re-executed from scratch under strictly controlled conditions:

  • Hardware & OS: Intel Core i5-8365U (4 physical cores / 8 logical processors, 1.60–1.90 GHz), Windows 64-bit.
  • Runtime Stack: Python 3.14.10, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, PySide6 6.10.2 (QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen).
  • CPU Contention Guard: System-wide CPU utilization was sampled via Win32 GetSystemTimes (kernel + user vs. idle ticks) before every benchmark block, waiting until background system CPU load settled between 1.6% and 15.5% (compared to ~83% system CPU utilization during the initial exploratory profiling session).
  • Execution Protocol:
  • Zero concurrent background tasks or parallel test processes were active during timing runs.
  • All modules (numpy, scipy, pandas, pybaselines, PySide6, spectroview.*) were pre-imported before timed sections so cold-import latency never contaminated warm execution metrics.
  • Every operation was executed with 1–2 warmup passes followed by 3–10 timed repetitions, recording min, median, and mean ± std.

docs.title: 1.2 Measurement Taxonomy Used in This Document
docs.text:
To prevent conflating different classes of numbers, every metric in this roadmap is explicitly labeled as one of four categories:

  1. [Measured — Current Baseline]: Direct multi-run time.perf_counter() / byte-footprint measurement of the unmodified SPECTROview v26.48.2 codebase under idle CPU conditions (1.6%–15.5% background load).
  2. [Measured — Isolated Prototype]: Direct multi-run measurement of a standalone in-memory prototype function implementing the proposed optimization on the exact same dataset and hardware during this audit (with numerical equivalence verified against the baseline).
  3. [Estimated — Integrated Workflow]: Projected end-to-end timing or memory footprint once the isolated prototype is wired into the full View ↔ ViewModel ↔ Model pipeline (accounting for remaining unoptimized stages via Amdahl's Law).
  4. [Theoretical — Asymptotic Scaling]: Mathematical complexity (\(O(\cdot)\) FLOPs or byte count) as dataset dimensions (\(N\) spectra, \(M\) channels, \(K\) parameters) scale.

docs.text:
• Location: spectroview/view/components/lists/v_spectra_list.py:170–221 (VSpectraList.set_spectra_names).

docs.title: Design & Touchpoints
docs.text:
1. SpectraListModel(QAbstractListModel) (v_spectra_list.py):
  2. Store lightweight parallel Python/NumPy sequences (_fnames: list[str], _is_active: np.ndarray, _has_baseline: np.ndarray, _has_fit: np.ndarray, _metadata: list[dict]) and an \(O(1)\) lookup dict _fname_to_row: dict[str, int].
  3. Implement rowCount(), data() (Qt.DisplayRole, Qt.CheckStateRole, Qt.BackgroundRole, Qt.ForegroundRole, Qt.UserRole), setData() (for checkbox toggles emitting spectrum_active_changed), and flags().
  4. Enable setUniformItemSizes(True) on the underlying QListView so Qt computes scrollbar geometry in \(O(1)\) without querying sizeHint() across all \(N\) rows.
  5. Preserve External VSpectraList API:
  6. Keep set_spectra_names(spectra: list[dict]), get_selected_fnames() -> list[str], set_selected_fnames(fnames: list[str]), drag-and-drop reordering, and all existing signals (spectra_selection_changed, spectrum_active_changed, context-menu actions) 100% backward compatible.

docs.text: Implementation Status (P2): Enforced C_CONTIGUOUS float32 Y0 in m_io.extract_map_arrays and SpectraStore.add_map (P2.1), eliminated the duplicate VMWorkspaceMaps.maps[name] float64 matrix by sharing md.Y0's float32 buffer (P2.2), preserved float32 across eval_baseline_batch / preprocessing / VBFthread Y_bestfit without allocating blank Y_baseline arrays (P2.3), and replaced eager 3D Y_peaks arrays with on-demand LazyPeakArray views (P2.4).

docs.title: Problem & Verified Evidence
docs.text:
• Locations:
  • spectroview/model/io/m_io.py:307–313 (extract_map_arrays)
  • spectroview/viewmodel/maps/vm_workspace_maps.py:72–115, 290–330
  • spectroview/model/spectra/spectra_store.py:23–115 (MapData)
  • spectroview/viewmodel/spectra/vm_workspace_spectra.py:1320–1390 (_on_fit_finished)
  • Verified Finding 1 — Fortran-Contiguous (F_CONTIGUOUS) Matrix Trap on .txt/.csv Maps:
  • When m_io.load_map_file() parses a .txt or .csv map (1_CL_map.txt, 16,384 × 1,024) via pd.read_csv(..., engine="c"), pandas stores the numeric block in column-major Fortran order (F_CONTIGUOUS=True, C_CONTIGUOUS=False).
  • In extract_map_arrays (m_io.py:310), Y0 = map_df.iloc[:, 2:].to_numpy().astype(np.float32, copy=False) preserves Fortran memory layout (strides = (4, 65536) on 16,384 × 1,024, whereas WdfReader produces C-contiguous strides = (2300, 4)).

docs.title: P3 — Algorithmic Optimization, OpenBLAS Thread Control & Background Threading for Multivariate Analysis (PCA & NMF)
Problem & Verified Evidence
docs.text:
• Location: spectroview/model/analysis/m_mva.py:75–201 (MMVA.run_pca, MMVA.run_nmf) and spectroview/viewmodel/analysis/vm_mva.py.
  • Three Compounding Root Causes Verified in Controlled Benchmarks:
  • OpenBLAS 8-Thread Oversubscription on 4 Physical Cores: By default, OpenBLAS spawns 8 threads on a 4-core / 8-thread CPU. Inside MMVA.run_nmf (200 iterations \(\times\) 6 matrix multiplications on narrow (1520, 4) and (4, 575) matrices = 1,200 micro-GEMMs), 8 OpenBLAS threads spin-wait at thread barriers across 4 cores, causing extreme OS scheduler jitter (min = 2,212.12 ms vs median = 7,283.42 ms, max = 12,681.25 ms). Setting OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2 alone cuts current NMF median time from 7,283.42 ms to 1,567.99 ms (4.65× speedup) and current SVD PCA median time from 2,471.73 ms to 652.80 ms (3.79× speedup)!
  • PCA Full Thin SVD Waste (m_mva.py:94): np.linalg.svd(X_centered, full_matrices=False) computes all \(\min(n, p) = 575\) singular vectors on an \((n, p)\) rectangular matrix even when n_components = 5. Forming the symmetric \((p \times p)\) covariance Gram matrix \(C = X_c^T X_c\) via BLAS dsyrk/dgemm and calling np.linalg.eigh(C) is mathematically equivalent and dramatically faster whenever \(n > p\).
  • NMF Explicit (N, M) Residual Allocation (m_mva.py:189): Every 10 iterations, MMVA.run_nmf computes error = np.linalg.norm(X - W @ H, "fro"), allocating a full (n, p) residual matrix even though numerator_W = X @ H.T, W.T @ W, and H @ H.T are already available for the \(O(K^2)\) Frobenius trace identity.
  • Controlled Multi-Run Measurements (1,520 × 575, float64):
Algorithm & Configuration Measurement Category min median mean ± std Numerical Parity vs. Current Baseline Measured Speedup (Median) MMVA.run_pca (k=5, current svd, default 8 BLAS threads) [Measured — Current Baseline] 1,033.34 ms 2,471.73 ms 2,446.76 ± 895.34 ms Reference 1.00× MMVA.run_pca (k=5, current svd, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 449.27 ms 652.80 ms 621.01 ± 91.33 ms Exact (0.0) 3.79× P3.1 Gram eigh(X_c.T @ X_c) (k=5, default 8 BLAS threads) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 129.83 ms 222.91 ms 198.92 ± 49.65 ms max_ev_diff = 3.73e-09 11.09× P3.1 Gram eigh(X_c.T @ X_c) (k=5, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 121.68 ms 125.65 ms 139.89 ± 28.48 ms max_ev_diff = 3.73e-09 19.67× MMVA.run_nmf (k=4, 200 it, current, default 8 BLAS threads) [Measured — Current Baseline] 2,212.12 ms 7,283.42 ms 7,392.26 ± 4,274.69 ms Reference 1.00× MMVA.run_nmf (k=4, 200 it, current, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 1,455.54 ms 1,567.99 ms 1,626.89 ± 170.51 ms Exact (0.0) 4.65× P3.2 Trace-identity + prealloc NMF (k=4, default 8 BLAS threads) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 974.51 ms 3,927.84 ms 4,824.14 ± 3,288.24 ms max_W_diff = 8.27e-05 1.85× P3.2 Trace-identity + prealloc NMF (k=4, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2) [Measured — Isolated Prototype] 548.04 ms 582.02 ms 587.07 ± 25.28 ms max_W_diff = 8.27e-05 12.51×

docs.title: Design & Touchpoints
docs.text:
1. P3.1 — Dual Covariance Gram Eigendecomposition in MMVA.run_pca (m_mva.py:75–133):
  2. When \(n > p\), compute \(C = X_c^T X_c\) (shape = (p, p)) and eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(C), sort descending ([::-1]), clamp tiny negative numerical noise with np.maximum(eigvals, 0.0), and recover all_eigenvalues = eigvals / (n - 1), loadings = eigvecs[:, :n_components].T, and scores = X_c @ loadings.T (applying deterministic sign canonicalization so the largest-magnitude loading entry per component is positive).
  3. When \(n \le p\), use the dual \((n \times n)\) Gram matrix \(C = X_c X_c^T\) with np.linalg.eigh(C) and recover unit-norm loadings via \(V_k = S_k^{-1} U_k^T X_c\).
  4. P3.2 — \(O(K^2)\) Frobenius Trace Identity & Preallocated Buffers in MMVA.run_nmf (m_mva.py:138–201):
  5. Precompute norm_X_sq = float(np.sum(X * X)) once before the loop and preallocate num_H, den_H, WtW, num_W, den_W, and HHt buffers using np.matmul(..., out=...).

  6. Every 10 iterations, refresh np.matmul(W.T, W, out=WtW) after updating W and evaluate:

    $\(\|X - WH\|_F = \sqrt{\max\left(0,\; \|X\|_F^2 - 2 \sum_{i,j} W_{i,j} (XH^T)_{i,j} + \sum_{a,b} (W^T W)_{a,b} (H H^T)_{a,b}\right)}\)$

  7. P3.3 — Application-Level OpenBLAS Thread Cap & Background QThread in VMMVA (main.py, vm_mva.py):

  8. In spectroview/__init__.py (before import numpy), set default os.environ.setdefault("OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS", "2") and os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "2") (or min(4, max(2, os.cpu_count() // 2))) so OpenBLAS never oversubscribes logical hyperthreads on 4-core laptops.
  9. Offload MMVA.run_pca and MMVA.run_nmf to a parented QThread worker in VMMVA when \(n \cdot p \ge 250{,}000\).

docs.title: P4 — VBF Engine, float32 Noise/Weight Pipeline & Analytical \(3 \times 3\) SPD Solver
Problem & Verified Evidence
docs.text:
• Locations:
  • spectroview/fit_engine/noise.py:14–85 (_array_2d_fingerprint, mad_noise, moving_average_5)
  • spectroview/fit_engine/weights.py:7–36 (compute_fit_weights)
  • spectroview/fit_engine/optimizer.py:45–75 (_batched_solve)
  • Verified Finding 1 — Mixed-Dtype Upcasting in moving_average_5 & Full-Array Sum in _array_2d_fingerprint:
  • In noise.py:69, moving_average_5(y) allocates out = np.empty((N, M), dtype=np.float64) even when y is float32, forcing 5 mixed-dtype (float64 += float32) strided ufunc passes (134.2 MB allocation instead of 67.1 MB).
  • In noise.py:25, _array_2d_fingerprint(y) computes float(np.sum(y)) across all 16,777,216 elements (12.50 ms per call \(\times 2\) calls = 25 ms overhead even on a cache hit, while compute_fit_weights takes 169.17 ms even on a cache hit because it allocates a 134.2 MB float64 weights array and scans two full (N, M) boolean masks!).
  • [Measured — Current Baseline] vs [Measured — Isolated Prototype] (16,384 × 1,024):
    • Current compute_fit_weights on F-contiguous Y_cl (float32): median = 2,355.58 ms (min = 2,054.62 ms).
    • Current compute_fit_weights on C-contiguous Y_cl (float32): median = 659.18 ms (min = 642.51 ms).
    • [Measured — Isolated Prototype P4.1] (C-contiguous float32 + float32-preserving moving_average_5 + strided y[::16, ::16] fingerprint): median = 483.46 ms (min = 453.84 ms, mean = 479.36 ± 16.59 ms, 0.000000 mask mismatch, 4.87× faster than current F-contiguous baseline and 1.36× faster than C-contiguous baseline).
  • Verified Finding 2 — Closed-Form Vectorized \(3 \times 3\) SPD Solver for 1-Peak Fits (\(K = 3\)):
  • For 1-peak Gaussian/Lorentzian fits (\(K = 3\)), _batched_solve calls general LAPACK dgesv (np.linalg.solve) on (Na, 3, 3) matrices.
  • [Measured — Current Baseline]: np.linalg.solve on (16,384 × 3 × 3) takes min = 6.84 ms | median = 9.76 ms | mean = 9.84 ± 2.02 ms.
  • [Measured — Isolated Prototype P4.2]: Direct vectorized \(3 \times 3\) symmetric cofactor/Cramer rule takes min = 1.36 ms | median = 1.54 ms | mean = 1.61 ± 0.25 ms (6.34× measured speedup, max_diff = 5.95e-14).
  • Verified Finding 3 — Effect of OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2 on VBF Batched LM Fits:
  • Because optimizer.py (since commit 9250ae9) chunks large maps into L3-cache sub-batches of 256–2,048 spectra, running OpenBLAS with 8 threads on 4 physical cores causes thread-barrier overhead inside each chunk's np.matmul(J_r_T, J_r) normal-equation step:
  • [Measured — Current Baseline] (1_CL_map.json, 16,384 × 302, 1 Lorentzian, K=3, default 8 BLAS threads): min = 3,385.22 ms | median = 3,433.74 ms (0.210 ms/spectrum).
  • [Measured — Isolated Prototype P4.3] (1_CL_map.json, 16,384 × 302, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2): 1,434.02 ms (0.088 ms/spectrum, 2.40× measured speedup, 100.0% converged, med_R2 = 0.9841)!

docs.text:
1. P4.1 (noise.py, weights.py):
  2. Preserve input float32/float64 dtype in moving_average_5(y) (out = np.empty((N, M), dtype=np.result_type(y.dtype, np.float32))).
  3. Replace full float(np.sum(y)) in _array_2d_fingerprint(y) with a constant-time strided sample float(np.sum(y[::max(1, n // 32), ::max(1, m // 32)], dtype=np.float64)) + corner/center elements.
  4. P4.2 (optimizer.py:_batched_solve):
  5. Add a fast closed-form \(3 \times 3\) symmetric solver branch when K == 3, falling back to _batched_solve general path if np.any(det <= 1e-18) or not np.all(np.isfinite(dp)).
  6. P4.3 (spectroview/__init__.py / optimizer.py):
  7. Cap default OpenBLAS/OMP threads to 2 (or physical core count \(\div 2\)) to eliminate the 2.40× multi-thread barrier penalty inside L3-chunked VBF fits.

docs.title: P5 — Background Worker & Multi-Core Acceleration for Batch Automatic Baselines (arpls, asls, snip)
Problem & Verified Evidence
docs.text:
• Location: spectroview/fit_engine/baseline.py:112–244 (eval_baseline, eval_baseline_batch) and spectroview/viewmodel/spectra/vm_workspace_spectra.py (subtract_baseline).
  • Controlled Idle-CPU Measurements (50 × 575 spectra from 3_3721map.wdf, [Measured — Current Baseline]):
  • Attached Linear (1,520 × 575): median = 30.61 ms (min = 29.76 ms, 0.020 ms/spectrum) — already fully vectorized.
  • Attached Polynomial (degree 3) (1,520 × 575): median = 30.79 ms (min = 29.05 ms, 0.020 ms/spectrum) — already fully vectorized.
  • Automatic asls (ALS) (50 × 575): median = 56.61 ms (min = 46.68 ms, 1.13 ms/spectrum \(\rightarrow\) [Estimated — Integrated Workflow] 1.72 s for 1,520 spectra).
  • Automatic arpls (50 × 575): median = 238.65 ms (min = 225.08 ms, 4.77 ms/spectrum \(\rightarrow\) [Estimated — Integrated Workflow] 7.25 s for 1,520 spectra).
  • Automatic snip (50 × 575): median = 378.88 ms (min = 349.80 ms, 7.58 ms/spectrum \(\rightarrow\) [Estimated — Integrated Workflow] 11.52 s for 1,520 spectra).
  • Important Negative Finding From Controlled Prototype Testing:
  • We explicitly benchmarked two candidate micro-optimizations on arpls (50 × 575):
    1. Hoisting Baseline(x_data=x) outside the per-spectrum loop in a single thread ([Measured — Isolated Prototype]: median = 263.38 ms, min = 226.85 ms vs 238.65 ms baseline — no speedup, because Baseline(x_data=x) initialization takes < 0.1 ms while 99% of time is spent inside scipy.linalg.solveh_banded during iterative Whittaker reweighting).
    2. Running ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) over hoisted Baseline(x_data=x) instances while OpenBLAS uses default threads ([Measured — Isolated Prototype]: median = 366.48 ms, min = 336.10 ms — 1.53× slower due to GIL contention inside pybaselines Python iteration loops and thread contention!).
  • Why This Matters: Recording this negative result prevents wasting engineering time on naive Baseline hoisting or ThreadPoolExecutor wrapping of pybaselines.

docs.title: Validated Design & Touchpoints
docs.text:
1. P5.1 — Non-Blocking QThread Execution for Batch Automatic Baselines (vm_workspace_spectra.py):
  2. Whenever subtract_baseline runs an automatic baseline mode (mode not in ("Linear", "Polynomial")) across \(N > 10\) spectra, execute eval_baseline_batch inside a parented QThread worker with a progress bar and cancel button (mirroring VBFthread).
  3. [Estimated — Integrated Workflow]: Main-thread UI freeze drops from 1.7–11.5 s to 0 ms.
  4. P5.2 — Vectorized Batch SNIP in Pure NumPy (baseline.py):
  5. The SNIP algorithm (Iterative decreasing/increasing window morphological clipping: \(y^{(p)}_{i,j} = \min(y^{(p-1)}_{i,j},\; 0.5 (y^{(p-1)}_{i,j-p} + y^{(p-1)}_{i,j+p}))\) for \(p = 1 \dots W\)) has zero data-dependent branching across spectra and can be written in 12 lines of 2D vectorized NumPy slice operations over the entire (N, M) matrix simultaneously!
  6. [Theoretical — Asymptotic Scaling]: Vectorizing 2D SNIP in NumPy eliminates \(N \times W\) Python loop iterations, reducing 1,520 × 575 SNIP from ~11.5 s to < 150 ms (~75× speedup).

docs.title: 1. Executive Summary
docs.text: An empirical audit and profiling study of SPECTROview's Vectorized Batch Fit (VBF) Engine was conducted across real Raman (3_3721map.wdf) and cathodoluminescence (1_CL_map.txt) hyperspectral datasets. The investigation explains why runtime escalates sharply when switching from Lorentzian to Pseudo-Voigt profiles or adding multiple overlapping peaks, and separates per-iteration computational cost from convergence-count inflation.

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
1. Benchmark Group A and Group B Test Different Spectra and Solver Tolerances:

  2. Group A (1_CL_map*.json) crops [319.70..480.79] (M=102 on 3_3721map.wdf, M=304 on 1_CL_map.txt). On 3_3721map.wdf, [319.70..480.79] is a signal-free region (med_peak = 6.81, frac_neg = 62.2%), causing unguided fitting into baseline noise (R²_med <= 0.00). On the intended dataset 1_CL_map.txt, real CL peaks sit near 387.7–394.8 (R²_med = 0.9841–0.9906).

  3. Group B (3_3721map*.json) crops [460.23..570.28] (M=71) or [460.23..579.64] (M=77), centered on the strong silicon Raman peak at 521.73 cm⁻¹ (med_peak = 6,695.98, R²_med = 0.9988–0.9996).

  4. Furthermore, 1_CL_map.json and 3_3721map.json use coef_noise = 1 (which zeroes all weights on signal-free spectra, skipping 3,477/3,721 fits on 3_3721map.wdf), whereas the multi-peak and Pseudo-Voigt configs set coef_noise = 0.0 (fitting every spectrum, including noise).

  5. Convergence Cost Dominates Multi-Peak Slowdowns (25× Iteration Multiplier), Amplified by Bound-Clipping:

  6. A single well-conditioned Lorentzian (3_3721map.json) or Pseudo-Voigt (3_3721map_1pseudo.json) converges in 4 iterations.

  7. Adding two weak satellite peaks alongside the Si peak (3_3721map_3Lorent.json, starting with Peak 1 at x0=497.15, a=0.0, w=0.10) stalls convergence: only 44/3,721 (1.2%) converge within max_ite = 100, forcing 99.3% mean active rows across all 100 iterations (a 25× iteration multiplier over the 1-peak case: 0.315 s -> 7.419 s).

  8. Verified Root Cause (P1.1): In optimizer.py, the convergence check measures np.abs(dp) before box-bound projection (np.clip(p_active + dp, lo, hi)). When any peak amplitude or PseudoVoigt alpha hits 0.0 (verified directly: 1,494 rows pinned at P1_alpha=0.0 on 1_CL_map_1pseudovoigt.json), |p_trial - p| == 0 and cost improvement is 0, yet the unconstrained Newton step dp remains nonzero, blocking convergence until max_ite. Fixing this single line yields a 4.14× speedup on 3_3721map_3Lorent.json (8.620 s -> 2.082 s, convergence rising from 44/3,721 to 3,486/3,721) and 1.84× on 1_CL_map_1pseudovoigt.json.

  9. Per-Iteration Cost Drivers (Fixed-10-Iteration Controlled Measurements):

  10. Why 1 Pseudo-Voigt is 3.18×–4.23× slower per iteration than 1 Lorentzian: batched_pseudovoigt() and batched_pseudovoigt_jac() recompute batched_gaussian(), batched_lorentzian(), batched_gaussian_jac(), and batched_lorentzian_jac() independently — recalculating dx, dx², 1/w², and normalized offset t² four times per Jacobian call and allocating temporary (N, M) and (N, M, 3) buffers before copying into (N, M, 4). Fixed-10-iteration cost grows 46.54 ms -> 148.13 ms (3.18×) on 3,721×77 and 576.95 ms -> 2,438.98 ms (4.23×) on 16,384×304.

  11. Why VBFevaluator.jacobian() accounts for ~50–60% of self+cumulative time: In cProfile, jacobian() spends more self time copying slices (_to_full(), np.zeros(), J_full[:, :, slc] = jac_fn(...), and fancy-index extraction J_full[:, :, self._free_idx]) than models.py spends computing derivatives. At N=16,384, M=304, 6_Lor (K=18) over 10 fixed iterations, JacCopy = 2,685.81 ms actually exceeds JacMath = 2,114.60 ms.
  12. _batched_solve() Cholesky Crossover Cliff (Na <= 500, K >= 10): As tail spectra stay active and drop below 501 rows while K >= 10, _batched_solve() switches from C batched np.linalg.solve to a Python loop calling scipy.linalg.cho_factor / cho_solve, creating a measured 5.7×–33.8× per-call regression (Na=450, K=12: 89.883 ms vs 2.661 ms).
  13. Working-Set Growth & Cache Spilling (O(N * M * K)): Holding full active tensors in DRAM instead of L2/L3 cache-sized batches forces repeated DRAM round-trips for residuals, Jacobians, and normal equations; additionally, full-axis dense evaluation wastes compute far outside localized Raman peaks.
  14. Cold Linear Baseline Import: First-ever invocation of Linear baseline fitting triggers a cold from scipy.interpolate import interp1d costing 1,508.64 ms (0.75 ms warm).

docs.title: 3. Priority 1 Action Plan (Immediate Target — High Impact, Low Complexity)
docs.text:
These five pure-NumPy/Python changes preserve existing public contracts, exact numerical precision (float64), and startup import deferral:

  • P1.1 (optimizer.py) — Post-Clip Projected-Step Convergence + Uniform-Weight Fast Path:

  • Compute dp_actual = p_trial_active[improved_active] - p_active[improved_active] (after np.clip box-bound projection) inside dp_rel rather than raw unconstrained dp. Note that p_active = p[active_idx] via integer array indexing is already a separate copy before p[improved_idx] is updated.

  • Detect once up front when weights is None or (weights == 1.0).all() to bypass weights * residuals and J_r *= weights[:, :, None] array passes.

  • P1.2 (optimizer.py) — Unify _batched_solve on Vectorized np.linalg.solve:

  • Always try np.linalg.solve(A, b[..., None])[..., 0] across all (Na, K, K) systems regardless of Na or K, eliminating the 5.7×–33.8× per-matrix Cholesky loop cliff at Na <= 500, K >= 10. Retain per-matrix cho_factor/np.linalg.solve/0.0 strictly inside the except np.linalg.LinAlgError fallback for singular edge cases.

  • P1.3 (models.py) — Fuse batched_pseudovoigt & batched_pseudovoigt_jac + Optional out= Buffer:

  • Share dx, inv_w, inv_w2, dx2, t2 = dx2 * inv_w2, g_unit = exp(-4*ln2*t2), and invD = 1 / (4*t2 + 1) inside single-pass fused batched_pseudovoigt and batched_pseudovoigt_jac.

  • Add optional out=None slice support to batched peak/Jacobian evaluators so VBFevaluator writes directly into preallocated buffers without per-peak allocations. Measured speedup: 1.71×–1.85×, numerical deviation max_abs_diff = 3.47e-12.

  • P1.4 (evaluator.py) — Zero-Copy VBFevaluator.jacobian() & evaluate() Free-Param Fast Path:

  • Precompute self._all_free_identity when no parameters are fixed (_fixed_idx is empty) and no parameter expressions (_exprs) exist.

  • Skip _to_full(), skip np.zeros() zero-initialization (every column 0..K-1 is partitioned cleanly by peak slices), pass out=J[:, :, slc] directly to peak evaluators, and return J without J_full[:, :, _free_idx] fancy-index copying. Support an optional caller-supplied out= buffer in evaluate() and jacobian() when not self._exprs.

  • P1.5 (evaluator.py, baseline.py) — O(N) Noise-Threshold Lookup & Pure-NumPy Linear Baseline:

  • Replace dists = np.abs(x[None, :] - x0_vals[:, None]) in VBFevaluator.apply_noise_threshold() with uniform fast-path (when x0 is identical across N) or np.searchsorted + neighbor compare on monotonic 1D x, cutting (N, M) memory down to O(N).

  • Implement closed-form vectorized linear interpolation/extrapolation (_interp_linear_extrap) in pure NumPy in baseline.py (eval_baseline() and eval_baseline_batch()), eliminating the 1,508.64 ms cold scipy.interpolate import overhead.

docs.title: 4. Phase 2 Implementation Plan (High Impact, Moderate Complexity)
docs.text: Phase 2 targets memory hierarchy efficiency, stalled-peak termination, localized spatial sparsity, and multi-core CPU scaling — all purely in Python/NumPy without native compiler toolchains.

docs.title: P2.1 — L3-Cache-Sized Batch Chunking & Active-Row Compaction [Partially Completed & Shipped in v26.48.1 — commit 9250ae9]
docs.text: Implementation Status (9250ae9, v26.48.1): Adaptive L3-cache batch chunking (_choose_chunk_size(N, M, K) in optimizer.py:21–42, chunked outer loop in optimizer.py:263–320 with monotonic weighted progress_callback), physical (K, N, M) Jacobian buffer transposed to (N, M, K) for unit-stride BLAS dgemm, in-place analytical derivatives in models.py, zero-copy all_active = (n_active == N) full-batch fast path, and 2D noise/moving-average memoization in noise.py are completed and shipped. Under controlled idle-CPU re-benchmarking (v26.48.2), WDF 3_3721map.json (3,721 × 70, K=3) improved from 157.6 ms (Phase 1) to 70.81 ms (63.67 ms with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2), and CL 1_CL_map.json (16,384 × 302, K=3) improved from 3,802.1 ms (Phase 1) to 3,433.74 ms (1,434.02 ms with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2). Only intra-chunk active-row sub-array compaction when 1 <= n_diverged < N_chunk remains open.

docs.title: Problem & Evidence
docs.text:
• Currently, batched_levenberg_marquardt() keeps global (N, M, K) Jacobian tensors (~114–684 MiB on N=16,384, M=304) and (N, K, K) caches for all N spectra simultaneously, even after 75–90% have converged or while active rows span fragmented memory indices.
  • Every iteration on non-contiguous active_idx pays cache misses across the full N-row allocation.
  • Empirically verified on 3_3721map.wdf / 3_3721map_3Lorent.json: splitting N=3,721 into chunk=512 reduced runtime from 8.254 s -> 4.942 s (1.67×) with max |ΔR²| = 2.22e-16.

docs.title: Design & Touchpoints (optimizer.py, vbf_engine.py)
docs.text:
1. Deterministic Adaptive Chunk Sizing (_choose_chunk_size(N, M, K)):

  2. Target a working set (chunk_size, M, K) * 8 bytes <= ~8–16 MiB (fitting comfortably inside L3 cache on typical 8–32 MiB CPU caches while staying big enough for BLAS matmul batch amortization).

  3. Clamp chunk_size in [256, 1024] (e.g., chunk_size = max(256, min(1024, (12 * 1024 * 1024) // max(M * max(K, 1) * 8, 1)))). If N <= chunk_size, run zero-split direct path to avoid overhead on small calls.

  4. Chunk Execution & Contiguous Active-Row Compaction:

  5. Slice (x_chunk, y_chunk, p0_chunk, w_chunk) into contiguous chunks [s:e], call _batched_lm_core(...), and write back into preallocated (N, K) p_out, (N,) converged, and (N,) n_iter arrays.

  6. Inside each chunk Nc <= 1024, compute noise/zero-weight masks locally. Once active count drops cleanly (or when active density < 0.5), optionally pack (p_c, residuals_c, JTJ_c, JTr_c, lam_c) into dense contiguous sub-arrays, avoiding scattered active_idx / dirty[active_idx] gather/scatter penalties.

  7. Note: Each spectrum in LM is mathematically 100% independent, so chunking preserves bit-exact parity (max |ΔR²| ~ 1e-16).

  8. Progress Reporting Integration (progress_callback):

  9. Maintain weighted completed-spectrum counts (completed_in_finished_chunks + converged_in_current_chunk) so UI progress bars inside VBFthread remain smooth and monotonic (0 -> 100%) instead of resetting per chunk.

docs.title: Risks & Validation
docs.text:
• Shared x vs 2D (N, M) x: Always slice x[s:e] when x.ndim == 2, pass x unmodified when x.ndim == 1.
  • Test: Assert chunked (chunk=256, 512) vs unchunked output parity (np.allclose on p, R², converged, n_iter) across 1D and 2D x, weights, and _exprs.

docs.title: P2.2 — Inactive / Bound-Pinned Peak Convergence & Stagnation Early Exit
Problem & Evidence
docs.text:
• Even after P1.1 fixes bound clipping for pixels pinned right at iteration t, multi-peak configurations with an absent/vanishing component (like Peak 1 x0=497.15, a=0.0 in 3_3721map_3Lorent or 2nd/3rd peak on background CL pixels) still suffer from ill-conditioned (J^T J) blocks: when ampli ≈ 0, derivatives \(\partial/\partial x_0 = 0\) and \(\partial/\partial w = 0\), leaving zero columns in J (rank < K) so LM spends dozens of iterations shrinking/growing damping \(\lambda\) before xtol/ftol triggers.
  • On 1_CL_map.txt / 1_CL_map_3lorentzian, ~22.6% of spectra still hit max_ite=100 (61.4 s even after P1.1 + P1.4).

docs.title: Design & Touchpoints (optimizer.py, fit_engine/)
docs.text:
1. Diagonal Tikhonov Floor / Zero-Column Safeguarding:

  2. In (JTJ + lam * diag(JTJ)), a dead peak with ampli == 0 yields diag(JTJ)[idx] == 0. Current lam * np.maximum(diag_JTJ, 1e-6) helps invertibility, but when a peak amplitude collapses to 0 (ampli <= lo_ampli + eps and gradient w.r.t. ampli points negative/outward), zeroing the trial steps of its coupled (x0, fwhm, alpha) parameters prevents spurious width/position drift and triggers immediate step acceptance or convergence (dp_actual == 0).

  3. Stagnation / Consecutive Rejected-Step Early Exit:

  4. Currently, a spectrum stops early only when lam >= 1e7 (optimizer.py:310) or when rel_cost_change < ftol & dp_rel < effective_xtol.

  5. Under floating-point precision plateaus near 1e-7..1e-12, tiny 1e-8 cost improvements can keep a row spinning at lam = 1e2..1e6 for 80+ iterations with zero physically meaningful movement.

  6. Add two safe early exits (configurable / preserving strict precision tests):

    • Plateau Exit: Track consecutive tiny-cost-and-tiny-step accepted iterations (e.g., rel_cost_change < ftol * 0.1 for 3 consecutive accepted steps -> converge).
    • Dead-Step Rejection Cap: Keep (worsened_active & lam_trial >= 1e7) while additionally terminating rows whose unconstrained np.linalg.norm(dp) would move < 1e-12 or which spend > 12 consecutive rejections without improvement.

  7. Optional Exact Backtracking / Nielsen LM Damping Update:

  8. Replace heuristic factor 10.0 / 3.0 (optimizer.py) with Nielsen's gain-ratio (rho) update (mu *= max(1/3, 1 - (2*rho - 1)**3), nu = 2 vs mu *= nu, nu *= 2), which reduces rejected step ratios on coupled multi-peak landscapes by avoiding premature damping spikes and overshoot restarts.

docs.title: Risks & Validation
docs.text: • Tight-tolerance unit tests: Any test expecting max_ite or exact tight xtol=1e-10 on synthetic noise-free problems must still pass — gate Nielsen / stagnation exits cleanly so xtol/ftol contracts are respected when tight tolerances are explicitly requested.

docs.title: P2.3 — Safe Support-Windowed Peak Evaluation (|x - x0| <= c * fwhm)
Problem & Evidence
docs.text:
• Raman and sharp luminescence spectra often span wide wave-number ranges (M = 500–2,000) where individual peaks have fwhm = 4–12 cm⁻¹. Away from |x - x0| > 6 * fwhm, Gaussian weights decay below 2^-144 (exact zero in float64), whereas Lorentzian tails decay slowly (\(1 / (1 + 4 (dx/w)^2)\): 1/65 ≈ 1.54% at 4*w and 1/10,001 ≈ 10⁻⁴ only at 50*w).
  • Benchmark from vbf_bench_part2.txt (6 Lorentzians, N=1681, M=1024, fwhm=6): dense float64 = 966.43 ms/iter vs +-4*w block-diagonal windowed 82.72 ms/iter (11.68×) when localized!

docs.title: Critical Mathematical Guardrail (Why Support Windowing Requires Care)
docs.text:
• Lorentzian / Asymmetric Lorentzian / PseudoVoigt have heavy algebraic tails (\(O((w/dx)^2)\)):

  • Cutting Lorentzian strictly at 4 * fwhm leaves a 1.54% truncation discontinuity if used directly on evaluate() / residuals. Even at 15 * fwhm, 1 / (1 + 4*225) = 0.0011 (0.11%).

  • Therefore, a naive hard cutoff on models.py for Lorentzian/PseudoVoigt without tail correction would distort broadband fits (R² drift on wide peaks).

  • Safe Design Strategy:

  • Exponential Models (Gaussian, GaussianAsym): Exact machine-epsilon cutoff exists at |dx / w| > 4.5 (exp(-4 * ln(2) * 4.5^2) = 3.1e-25 < eps_float64). A slice/index window around [min(x0) - 5*max(w), max(x0) + 5*max(w)] for each chunk/peak group is mathematically exact to machine precision (< 1e-16).

  • All-Peak ROI Tight-Mask Prefilter (vbf_engine.py / VBFevaluator): Within any chunk, compute [lo_chunk, hi_chunk] across active centers ± tail tolerance; when peaks all occupy a narrow active sub-band inside an uncropped spectrum (or when DecaySingleExp/DecayBiExp only operate post-t0), restrict evaluation slice [i0:i1] for Jacobian & residual assembly.
  • Opt-In Fast Preview vs Exact Final Polish: Optionally use narrower fast support (8 * fwhm) during coarse early iterations if exposed as a precision mode, followed by full-band exact LM polish (1–2 iterations) to eliminate tail bias completely (ΔR² == 0.0).

docs.title: P2.4 — BLAS Thread Control & Persistent Warm Worker Pool
Problem & Evidence
docs.text:
• BLAS Oversubscription (vbf_bench_part2.txt, Section G): Running 2dmap_spc_bl 3p(25it) across OpenBLAS/OMP thread counts showed:

  • 1 thread: 10,874.9 ms

  • 2 threads: 9,493.7 ms (optimal)
  • 4 threads: 10,306.8 ms
  • 8 threads: 14,646.2 ms (54% slower due to thread barrier spin on small (chunk, M, K) GEMMs!)
  • Multiprocessing (audit_wdf_part3.txt): Spawning cold ProcessPoolExecutor on Windows took 10.39 s (w=4) and 12.79 s (w=8) vs 8.33 s single-process (0.80× / 0.65× regression) on 3_3721map_3Lorent due to Python interpreter startup & DLL load (~2–4 s per worker!). Conversely, a pre-warmed pool (w=4) achieved 1.95× (4.27 s) on 3_3721map and 1.83× (7.56 s) on 1_CL_map_1pseudovoigt.

docs.title: Design & Touchpoints (fit_engine/, application/, requirements optional threadpoolctl)
docs.text:
1. Scoped Single/2-Thread BLAS Guard (via threadpoolctl if installed, no hard dependency):

  2. Inside batched_levenberg_marquardt() (when chunked or inside worker processes), wrap execution with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(limits=2) (or limits=1 inside multi-process workers) using try ... except ImportError: so it fails gracefully when threadpoolctl is absent. Never call at startup (test_startup_imports.py).

  3. Lazy Persistent Worker Pool (VBFProcessPool, Optional Thresholded N * M * K):

  4. Spawn workers lazily on first large map fit (or warm asynchronously after UI load) rather than per-fit cold teardown, keeping w = min(4, max(1, cpu_count // 2)) workers capped to avoid RAM duplication.

  5. Only dispatch across IPC when total problem cost (N * M * K) exceeds a calibrated threshold (e.g., estimated_flops > threshold, skipping IPC entirely for fast < 1 s fits where chunked single-process finishes before IPC overhead completes).
  6. Keep every worker single-threaded (limits=1) in BLAS/OMP so 4 workers × 1 thread never oversubscribes physical cores.
  7. Guard carefully for PyInstaller frozen executables on Windows/macOS (multiprocessing.freeze_support(), picklable pure-NumPy inputs/functions without Qt objects — note VBFevaluator expressions _exprs must either serialize cleanly as raw config dicts rebuilt per worker or stay in-process if custom lambdas exist).

docs.title: 5. Phase 3 Implementation Plan (Advanced Architectural & Algorithmic Improvements)
docs.text: Phase 3 narrows the remaining architectural gap between Python/NumPy tensor batching and compiled L1-resident single-spectrum C++ loops (such as HORIBA LabSpec 6's OlMainer.dll).

docs.title: P3.1 — Optional Compiled Native C++/OpenMP L1-Resident Kernel (Cross-Platform)
Architectural Rationale
docs.text:
Why can a compiled C++ loop (OpenMP parallel for per spectrum) beat whole-map Python tensor ops even when NumPy calls BLAS/C?

  • Cache Residency: For one spectrum of size M = 100..500, K = 3..18, the working set (x, y, r, J, JTJ, JTr) is ~10–80 KiB — fitting 100% inside per-core L1/L2 CPU cache, never hitting DRAM inside the LM loop.
  • Loop Fusion: Evaluating f(x), r, J, AND accumulating symmetric upper triangle of JᵀJ (0.5 * K * (K+1) entries) and Jᵀr inside a single streaming pass over i = 0..M-1 eliminates (N, M, K) memory materialization completely (from ~684 MiB peak DRAM down to < 1 MiB!) and fuses transcendental exp() SIMD instructions with normal-equation GEMM.
  • Zero Per-Iteration Barrier: Each CPU thread iterates its own subset of spectra cleanly to convergence with zero inter-iteration synchronization and zero active-mask compaction.

docs.title: Implementation Blueprint
docs.text:
1. Backend Design: Write a clean, portable C++17 + OpenMP (using PyBind11 or Cython) module _vbf_native covering:

  2. Built-in peak kernels (Gaussian, Lorentzian, PseudoVoigt, GaussianAsym, LorentzianAsym, Fano, DecaySingleExp, DecayBiExp) — no arbitrary Python string callbacks inside the hot C++ loop.

  3. Direct Cholesky (LL^T) / LDL^T symmetric positive-definite linear solver on stack-allocated <= 64×64 buffers (matching VBF's setStackSize lesson — fixed small stack buffers or per-thread heap scratch reused across all spectra).

  4. Identical parameterization, bounds clipping, linear/soft_l1/huber robust weights, and ftol/xtol/max_ite convergence semantics matching optimizer.py.

  5. Hybrid Dispatch & Automatic Fallback:

  6. In VBFengine.fit_spectra(): check not evaluator._exprs and all peak models supported by native kernel + _vbf_native importable (try: import spectroview.fit_engine._vbf_native).

  7. Otherwise seamlessly fall back to Phase 1/2 NumPy/Python optimizer.py (which continues supporting arbitrary user _exprs, dynamic/custom scalar models, and pure-Python environments without a C compiler).

  8. Packaging & Cross-Platform Distribution:

  9. Distribute prebuilt Python wheels (cibuildwheel in CI) for Windows x64, macOS arm64/x64 (libomp), and Linux x64 so end-users never require build tools locally; keep SPECTROview 100% runnable in pure Python if the compiled extension isn't built in dev mode.

docs.title: P3.2 — Variable Projection (VarPro / Separable Nonlinear Least Squares) & Optional Spatial Warm-Start
Mathematical & Algorithmic Concept
docs.text:
Every spectroscopic multi-peak sum is linear in peak amplitudes \(a_1, \dots, a_P\) given nonlinear shape parameters \(\theta = \{(x_{0,p}, w_p, \alpha_p)\}_{p=1}^P\):

\[\mathbf{y} \approx \sum_{p=1}^{P} a_p \phi_p(\mathbf{x}; \theta_p) = \Phi(\theta) \mathbf{a}\]

  1. Variable Projection (VarPro):

  2. Instead of optimizing \(K = 3P\) (or \(4P\)) parameters jointly (where strongly correlated overlapping peak amplitudes oscillate with widths/centers and produce poorly conditioned JᵀJ), reduce LM unknowns to nonlinear shape parameters only (\(2P\) or \(3P\), e.g. 6 instead of 9 for 3 Lorentzians, 9 instead of 12 for 3 Pseudo-Voigts — reducing \(K^3\) solve cost by ~3× and conditioning dramatically).

  3. For each spectrum trial \(\theta\), solve the small non-negative / unconstrained \((P \times P)\) system \(\Phi^T \Phi \mathbf{a} = \Phi^T \mathbf{y}\) (or Kaufman's approximated VarPro Jacobian for \(\theta\)).

  4. Requires careful handling of fixed/expressed amplitudes and upper/lower amplitude bounds (nnls or bounded active-set when lo/hi constrain amplitudes); therefore suited as a well-tested specialized solver path for standard unbounded/non-negative sum-of-peaks models.

  5. Optional Spatial Warm-Start Propagation (Grid-Aware Coarse Sweep -> Batched Refine):

  6. On smoothly varying Raman/wafer maps (x_coord, y_coord), spectra close in space often share very similar peak centers/widths while p0 builds a single global scalar guess across all N rows.

  7. Instead of sequential spiral fitting (which destroys parallelism), use a 2-stage parallel refinement:

    1. Fit a coarse downsampled grid (e.g. every \(4 \times 4\) tile or \(k\)-means spectral cluster centroids, ~5% of spectra) cleanly to convergence.
    2. Broadcast/bilinearly interpolate converged parameters to initialize the remaining 95% of pixels, which then run in 1 fully vectorized batched LM pass (typically converging in 2–4 iterations instead of 30–100).
    3. Must stay strictly opt-in or map-only (MapData with uniform spatial grid / spectral clustering fallback) with careful handling of domain boundaries / discontinuities (e.g., defects or empty substrate regions via residual-gated acceptance: keep spatial seed only if cost(spatial_p0) < cost(default_p0)!).

docs.title: P3.3 — Vectorized Forward-Mode Dual-Number AD for Linked Expressions (_exprs) [Completed & Shipped in v26.48.1 — commit 9250ae9]
docs.text: Implementation Status (9250ae9, v26.48.1): Fully completed and shipped in spectroview/fit_engine/evaluator.py via _DualVar, _DUAL_SAFE_NAMESPACE, topological expression bytecode compilation (_compiled_expr_ops), and batched np.matmul chain-rule combination (2.97× speedup over finite-difference chain-rule loops), verified by unit tests in tests/unit/fit_engine/test_evaluator.py.

docs.title: Problem & Evidence
docs.text:
• Currently (2dmap_spc.spc | 3p_expr, vbf_bench_report.txt), linking 2 parameters via _exprs (K_free = 7 < K_total = 9) caused jac time to balloon from 42.37 s (53.4%) to 75.73 s (68.9%) despite solving smaller 7×7 normal equations!
  • Why? VBFevaluator._build_chain_rule_expr_funcs() numerically finite-differences every expression function per free parameter on each Jacobian evaluation (evaluator.py).

docs.title: Design (evaluator.py)
docs.text:
• Implement a lightweight vectorized DualTensor(val, deriv) class over NumPy arrays supporting arithmetic (+, -, *, /, **) and standard math ufuncs (sin, cos, exp, log, sqrt, abs, minimum, maximum) restricted to safe AST-evaluated math namespaces.
  • Evaluate each compiled parameter expression once on (p_free_i, eye_k) DualTensors to obtain exact machine-precision analytical chain-rule derivatives \(\partial p_{\text{dep}} / \partial p_{\text{free}}\) across all N spectra in one vectorized pass — completely eliminating nested finite-difference sweeps and improving Jacobian accuracy for tightly constrained crystallographic/phonon doublet ratios.

docs.title: 6. Verification Gates for Future Phase 2 & Phase 3 Work
docs.text:
Every optimization milestone in Phase 2 and Phase 3 must pass the following gates before merge:

  1. Numerical Equivalence: On noiseless and real-data reference maps (3_3721map.wdf, 1_CL_map.txt, 2dmap_spc.spc, mapls6.l6m), verify converged parameter agreement, bounded parameter constraints, and median/p10 \(R^2\) fidelity (\(\Delta R^2 \le 10^{-6}\) for exact rewrites; documented trade-offs for approximate/surrogate modes).
  2. Startup Import Deferral: Pass tests/performance/test_startup_imports.py (scipy.*, optional threadpoolctl, or heavy modules never imported at top-level startup).
  3. Full Test Suite & Static Check: Pass python -m pytest tests/ -q and python -m pyflakes on all modified modules.
  4. Reproducible Before/After Benchmark Table: Measure and record wall time, ms/spectrum, peak tracemalloc heap, iteration count, and convergence fraction on both 3_3721map.wdf and 1_CL_map.txt.

docs.title: AI Chat Agent
docs.text:
The SPECTROview AI Agent is a built-in AI assistant that lets you query, filter, visualize, and modify your data using plain natural language — no coding required.

The AI Chat Agent is optional. SPECTROview works fully without it. You only need to set it up if you want to use AI-powered features.

Talk to SPECTROview in plain language to filter data and create or customize plots.

docs.title: 1. Opening the AI Chat Agent
docs.text:
You can toggle the embedded AI Chat panel in two ways:

  • Click the AI Chat Agent button on the right side of the top menu bar (placed right before Check for updates).
  • Use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + Shift + A.

The panel is embedded directly on the far right side of the main GUI, next to the workspace tab widget (Spectra, Maps, Graphs). You can drag the splitter handle to adjust its width freely, or click the close button (✕) in the panel header to hide it and give full width back to the workspaces.

docs.title: 2. Supported Providers
docs.text:
The AI Agent supports multiple LLM backends out of the box — no extra packages to install:

Provider Description Requires Ollama (local) Fully local, no internet, no API key Ollama installed and running OpenAI GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, etc. API key DeepSeek Cost-effective, high-quality reasoning DeepSeek API key Gemini Google Gemini models Gemini API key Mistral Mistral AI models Mistral API key Anthropic Claude models Anthropic API key Custom Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (e.g. an internal/institutional server) Base URL + API key

Note: DeepSeek, Gemini, and other OpenAI-compatible providers all use the openai Python package as a generic networking client. You are not sending data to OpenAI — only the package is reused as a universal API tool.

docs.title: 3. Configuring a Provider and Model
docs.text:
1. Inside the Chat Composer at the bottom of the panel, select an AI Provider from the dropdown (Ollama (local), OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Custom).
  2. For cloud providers, configure your API key in the Settings dialog (Ctrl + Shift + S → AI Settings tab):
  3. The Custom provider's Custom API Key, Base URL, and Model Name(s) fields are shown by default.
  4. Other cloud provider keys are organized under the collapsed ▸ Other cloud providers section.
  5. Use the Test Connection button directly in the AI Settings tab to verify authentication, host connectivity, and model availability with immediate visual feedback (✓ Connection successful or detailed error messages).
  6. Choose a Model from the editable model dropdown right next to the provider in the composer toolbar. If your model is not listed, you can type its identifier directly.
  7. Click the ⟳ refresh button next to the model dropdown to refresh available models.

Model Name & Label: Some endpoints (custom ones especially) do not expose a model-listing API. Enter the model names you use in Settings → AI Settings tab → Model Name(s) as a comma-separated list (e.g. model-a, model-b). You can also specify a custom Display Label (e.g. ABC or Lab Model) so that your endpoint appears by name in the composer's provider dropdown instead of generic Custom. Settings changes are applied immediately to any open chat panel.

docs.title: 4. Automatic Small-Model Optimization
docs.text: Small local models (roughly under ~10 billion parameters — such as qwen2.5:7b, gemma2:2b, phi3:mini) are noticeably more sensitive to long system prompts. SPECTROview automatically inspects the parameter size of local Ollama models and activates a compact prompt tier, a targeted conversation window, and tuned generation parameters.

docs.title: 5. Modern Chat Composer & Interface Overview
docs.text:
The chat interface features an intuitive, unified layout:

  • Top Header Bar: A clean, single-row header bar containing the editable Conversation Title on the left (takes available width) and quick-action icon buttons on the right: Chat History, New Chat, Clear Chat, and Close Panel (✕).
  • Conversation Thread: Displays color-coded message cards (User, AI replies with formatted Markdown/tables/equations, and error alerts).
  • Embedded Composer Card: A rounded composer box at the bottom containing:
  • An auto-expanding multi-line text input (press Enter to send, Shift + Enter for new lines).
  • An embedded bottom toolbar hosting the AI Provider selector, Model selector, Refresh button, Voice dictation mic (🎤), and Send ▶ / Stop ■ button.

docs.title: Conversation History Dialog
docs.text:
Clicking the Chat History icon button opens a management dialog inspired by PLUME:

  • Search filter: Real-time text search across conversation titles.
  • Section organization: Pinned conversations are organized at the top under a PINNED section; others are grouped chronologically (TODAY, YESTERDAY, THIS WEEK, OLDER).
  • Exact Timestamps & Message Counts: Each conversation card displays precise timestamping (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS) and message counts.
  • Actions: Pin/Unpin, Rename, Duplicate, and Delete conversations via dedicated row action buttons or right-click context menu.
  • Safe Delete All: The Delete All button cleans up unpinned conversations while safely keeping pinned items.

The chat panel shows messages in chronological order with clear color-coded bubbles:

  • 🔵 Blue bubble — Your messages (User)
  • 🟢 Green bubble — AI Agent replies
  • 🔴 Red bubble — Error messages

Each bubble shows the timestamp (YY-MM-DD HH:MM) and action buttons:

  • 📋 Copy — Copy the message text to clipboard
  • ↩ Reply (AI messages only) — Reply specifically to that AI message

docs.title: 🎤 Voice Dictation (Optional)
docs.text:
You can use the microphone button in the input bar to dictate your queries instead of typing them. This feature requires optional dependencies: 

pip install SpeechRecognition pyaudio
If these are not installed, the microphone button will still appear but will show an error message when clicked instructing you to install them.

docs.title: 6. What the AI Agent Can Do
docs.text:
The AI Agent has full awareness of your loaded DataFrames and open graphs. It can:

  • Filter data: Show rows matching any condition
  • Compute statistics: Mean, std, min, max, percentiles
  • Create plots: Generate any of the 9 supported plot styles
  • Modify graphs: Update axis ranges, titles, colors, filters
  • Delete graphs: Remove specific or all open graphs
  • Answer questions: Explain column contents, suggest analysis steps

The agent always knows your DataFrame names and every column name and type. It looks up the rest — example values from a column, or a graph's exact current settings — only when a question needs them, so ordinary requests stay fast.

docs.title: 🚀 Complex / Combined Prompts
docs.text:
The real strength of the agent is handling rich, multi-step requests in a single message — analyze the data, create several graphs, and fine-tune their appearance all at once.

Analyze, then plot: 

Compute the mean and std of center_Si per Zone, then create a bar plot of the
per-Zone mean with error bars from the std, sorted from highest to lowest.

Find the wafer with the highest average FWHM_Si, filter to just that wafer, and
plot a wafer map of its FWHM_Si.

Multiple graphs in one prompt: 

Create three graphs: a scatter of Slot vs center_Si colored by Zone, a box plot
of center_Si grouped by Zone, and a histogram of center_Si with 40 bins.

For each of FWHM_Si, center_Si and intensity_Si, plot a point plot vs Slot
colored by wafer.

Plot and customize in the same request: 

Make a scatter plot of Slot vs center_Si colored by Zone, set the title to
"Si peak position", label the Y-axis "Raman shift (cm⁻¹)", set the Y range to
[520, 522], use the viridis palette, and turn on the grid.

Plot FWHM_Si vs temperature as a trendline, filter to Zone == "center", move the
legend to the upper right, and use a log scale on the X-axis.

Everything together: 

Filter the data to R_squared > 0.95, then create a scatter plot and a box plot
of center_Si vs Zone side by side, colored by wafer, both with the title
"High-quality fits only" and the grid enabled.

docs.title: 🧩 Simple / Single-Action Prompts
docs.text:
Good starting points that each do one thing — filter, summarize, plot, tweak, or ask. Combine them freely into the complex prompts above.

Show rows where FWHM_Si > 5 and R_squared > 0.95

Give me statistics for center_Si and FWHM_Si by Zone

Create a scatter plot of Slot vs center_Si colored by Zone

Plot a wafer map of fwhm_Si for Slot 11
(Note: Wafer and 2Dmap plots require your dataset to have spatial X and Y coordinate columns). 
Set the Y-axis range of graph 3 to [3.5, 4.2] and use the viridis palette

Delete graph 3

What columns are available in my data?

docs.title: 8. Conversation History
docs.text:
The AI Agent remembers your conversation across multiple turns:

User: Show rows where FWHM > 5
AI:   Found 42 rows...

User: Now create a scatter plot of Slot vs center_Si for those rows
AI:   (creates scatter plot with FWHM > 5 filter applied)
  • The chat history is preserved when you load new files or switch datasets — it only resets when you click ➕ New Chat.
  • Past conversations are automatically saved and can be reopened from the History panel (📋 button).
  • Use ↩ Reply on any AI message to specifically respond to that turn.

docs.title: 9. Tips & Best Practices
docs.text:
• Be specific about column names — the AI knows your column names, but using the exact name avoids confusion.
  • Reference graph IDs — when modifying or deleting graphs, check the graph ID shown in its title bar.
  • Start simple — ask for a basic plot first, then refine it in follow-up messages.
  • Multiple plots at once — request several styles in one prompt: "Create a box and scatter plot of X vs Y".
  • Check the status bar — a 🔴 red indicator means the connection is not working. Check your API key in Settings or verify Ollama is running.
  • Struggling local model? — see section 4, keep requests to one or two plots per message, and prefer models that are explicitly documented as supporting tool/function calling.

docs.title: 10. Troubleshooting a "Connection error."
docs.text:
If a cloud/custom provider replies with "Connection error.", the app couldn't establish the network connection at all (it is not a wrong model name or an expired key — those report differently). Common causes:

  • Wrong Base URL — for a Custom provider, double-check the Base URL in Settings. It must be the endpoint's OpenAI-compatible root (e.g. https://host/v1 or https://host/openai/), not the full .../chat/completions path.
  • Corporate / internal endpoint with a private certificate — an on-premise endpoint (e.g. https://…intra.company…/) is often secured by a company certificate authority that Python doesn't trust by default, producing a hidden certificate verify failed error. SPECTROview handles this automatically by trusting your operating system's certificate store (via the truststore package, installed by default). If it still fails, point the app at your organization's certificate bundle by setting the environment variable SSL_CERT_FILE to your .pem file (e.g. chain_bundle.pem) before launching.
  • Off the network / VPN — an internal endpoint is only reachable from the corporate network or VPN.

The error card now shows the underlying cause (e.g. CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED, getaddrinfo failed) beneath the summary, which tells you which of the above applies.

docs.title: 11. Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl + Shift + A Open AI Chat Agent Enter Send message Shift + Enter New line in input box

docs.title: Quick Calculation Tool
docs.text: Click the Calculator icon in the Menu Bar to open a suite of utility calculators:

docs.title: 1. Laser Spot Size, Depth of Field, and Laser Power Density
docs.text:
This tool estimates the theoretical, diffraction-limited spatial resolution of your optical setup, including the spot size, depth of focus, and laser power density.

  • Spot Size: Calculated as 1.22 × λ / NA (μm)
  • Depth of Focus: Calculated as 4 × n × λ / NA2 (μm)

docs.title: 2. Penetration Depth
docs.text:
This tool calculates the theoretical optical penetration depth of a laser into a specific material, derived from its complex refractive index (extinction coefficient).

  • Penetration Depth (d): Calculated as λ / (4πk) (nm)

docs.title: 3. Unit Converter
docs.text: A rapid utility to convert between various standard spectroscopic units, ensuring seamless consistency during data analysis (e.g., converting wavelength in nm to energy in eV, or calculating Raman shift in cm-1 from excitation wavelengths).

docs.title: Workspace: Graphs
docs.text:
The Graphs workspace is exclusively dedicated to data visualization, engineered with a strong emphasis on simplicity, speed, and customization.

Overview of the Graphs Workspace interface.

docs.title: 1. Loading Data
docs.text:
Datasets can be passed seamlessly from the Spectra and Maps workspaces, or imported directly from external Excel/CSV files. All available datasets are dynamically tracked and displayed in the dataset list widget.

The four available utility buttons allow you to:

  • View: Inspect the data table natively.
  • Delete: Remove the dataset from the workspace.
  • Save: Export the dataset to Excel or CSV.
  • Refresh: Dynamically reload the CSV/Excel file if it has been modified externally.

docs.title: 2. Add or Update a Plot
docs.text:
1. Select your target dataset from the list.
  2. Choose the appropriate columns for the X, Y, and Z axes using the provided dropdown menus.
  3. Select your desired plot style (available styles: scatter, point, bar, box, line, trendline, histogram, 2Dmap, wafer).
  4. Define your plot labels, axis limits, and wafer diameter dimensions (if applicable).
  5. Click Add Plot to generate the visualization.
Demonstration of adding a new plot or updating an existing one.

docs.title: 3. The Shared Graph Toolbar
docs.text:
The bottom bar of the workspace hosts every global control plus one shared graph toolbar that always acts on whichever plot window is currently active. To make a plot active: click it, or pick it from the Active plot dropdown in the side panel (just above Add plot / Update plot).

Control Description Delete all Removes every plot from the workspace. Minimize all Minimizes every plot window. Undo / Redo Steps backward/forward through the workspace's edit history (Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z). Compose Figure Combines several open plots into one multi-panel exported figure. Home / Pan / Zoom / Subplots Standard Matplotlib navigation: reset the view, pan, zoom to a rectangle, or adjust subplot margins.

Tip: When you resize or move a plot window by dragging its edge or title bar, you see an outline first. The plot is redrawn once, at its new size, when you release the mouse. This keeps resizing smooth even for large plots. In the same way, while you pan, the margins around the axes stay fixed and are recalculated when you release the mouse.

A vertical separator marks where the plot's own controls start — always aligned to the right edge of the window:

Control Description Replicate Creates a duplicate of the active plot. Customize Opens the Customize Graph Dialog for the active plot (Ctrl+E, see below). Copy Copies the active plot's figure to the clipboard as an image (Ctrl+C). Export Click to export the active plot to file. Hold Ctrl + Click to export every open plot at once instead. Style menu (🎨) Save/apply a style, copy/paste style (Ctrl+V to paste), reset to default, or set the current style as the default for new plots.

Note: Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, and Ctrl+E above only work while the Graphs tab is the active tab — they won't interfere with the same shortcuts elsewhere in the app (e.g. typing in a text field).

docs.title: 4. Customizing a Plot
docs.text:
You can quickly modify the labels of the axes and the title of the plot via the Right Panel. Click the Update Plot button to apply the changes instantly:

Customize the selected plot via the Right Panel. Click the Update Plot button to apply changes.

For advanced customization, click the Customize button (⚙) to open the Customize Graph Dialog (Ctrl + E). The dialog features a modern Settings-like two-panel interface with real-time global search across all options, responsive left category navigation, and in-page option highlighting with automatic scroll-to-view across seven modular categories:

  • General & Typography: Figure theme (Light/Dark), Grid lines, X-axis label rotation, font sizes (Title, Axis label, Tick label, Colorbar), and intelligent data sorting.
  • Axes & Limits: Axis limits with interactive range sliders (on top), primary X/Y/Z scales (Linear, Logarithmic, Symlog, Centered), numerical/categorical data types, axis inversion, and broken axis ranges.
  • Ticks & Spines: Tick mark direction, tick label formatting presets, minor ticks (Top, Bottom, Left, Right), and spine frame border visibility.
  • Legend & Series: Legend box placement (inside/outside), borders, columns count, title, font size, alpha transparency, location, global marker styling, and left-aligned per-series styling table.
  • Plot Style & Fitting: Specialized plot options (join points, dodge points, wafer stats), unified error bar controls (show, statistic type, capsize), trendline polynomial fitting with anchor points and live equation tables, and histogram binning/KDE curves.
  • Annotations: Visual plot annotations (V-Line, H-Line, Text, Arrow, V-Span, H-Span, Box, Callout) with interactive canvas dragging and modal editing.
  • Secondary & Inset Axes: Secondary twin axes (Y2, Y3, X2 with dedicated labels, limits, log scales, colors, and markers) and Inset zoom sub-axes with connector lines.

All changes across tabs are applied together via the unified Apply button at the bottom of the dialog, or discarded via Cancel.

docs.title: 4.1 Axes & Limits, Ticks & Spines, and Secondary & Inset Axes
docs.text:
Axis configuration in the Customize Graph Dialog.

The Axes & Limits, Ticks & Spines, and Secondary & Inset Axes categories control axis scaling, data types, limits, tick/spine appearance, axis breaks, inset (zoom) axes, and secondary twin axes. Font sizes for titles/labels/ticks live in the General & Typography category.

docs.title: Axis Properties (Axes & Limits)
docs.text:
Configure the scale and data type for each axis independently using dropdown menus:

Setting Options Description X / Y axis Scale Linear, Logarithmic, Symlog Switches the axis between linear, logarithmic, and symmetric logarithmic scale. Logarithmic scale is only applied when the underlying data is numeric. X / Y axis Data type Auto, Category, Numerical Controls how axis values are interpreted. Auto (default): the application auto-detects the best type — numerical if 100% of the data is numeric, otherwise categorical. Category: forces categorical indexing. Numerical: forces a continuous numeric scale. Z axis Scale (wafer / 2Dmap only) Linear, Logarithmic, Centered Sets the color-scale normalization of the heatmap. Logarithmic compresses a wide range of values (falls back to linear if the data isn't strictly positive). Centered pins the colormap midpoint to a Center value you enter — ideal for diverging data such as stress/strain around 0.

Note: When using Numerical data type, the axis adopts a true mathematical scale where spacing reflects actual data values. When using Category, each unique value is evenly spaced regardless of its numeric magnitude.

docs.title: Set Axis Limits (Axes & Limits)
docs.text:
Manually constrain the visible range of each axis (X, Y, Z) by specifying min and max values:

Control Description X / Y / Z axis limits Enter min and max values to constrain the visible range. Leave a spinbox unset (it shows the plot's real current value, grayed out) to keep that side automatic. Get current limits from plot Captures the current visible limits from the plot and fills the spinboxes. Useful as a starting point before fine-tuning. Clear limits Resets all axis limits back to automatic (unconstrained). Adjusting the axis limits of the selected plot.

docs.title: Axis Appearance (Ticks & Spines)
docs.text: Control Description Minor ticks (X Bottom/Top, Y Left/Right) Enable minor tick marks on each edge of the plot independently. By default, minor ticks are automatically enabled only for axes representing numerical values (e.g., both X and Y for scatter/line/histogram plots, Y for bar/box/point plots) and hidden on categorical axes or map plots. Users can toggle minor ticks on or off for any axis independently. Show spines (Top/Right/Bottom/Left) Toggle visibility of each of the four plot border lines independently. Tick direction Default, In, Out, or In & Out. Tick label format Auto, Integer, 1-decimal, 2-decimal, or Scientific.

docs.title: Broken Axis (Axes & Limits — Beta)
docs.text:
Create a visual break in an axis to omit an uninteresting range and focus on relevant data regions:

Control Description X-axis break Enable and specify the from / to range to break on the X axis. Y-axis break Enable and specify the from / to range to break on the Y axis.

Note: This feature is in beta. Axis breaks work best with linear scales.

docs.title: Inset (Zoom) Axes (Secondary & Inset Axes)
docs.text:
Draw a small zoomed-in view of a region of the plot inside the main plot area:

Control Description Enable inset axes Turns the inset view on/off. Position (x0, y0) / Size (w, h) Placement and size of the inset box, as a fraction of the plot area (0–1). X / Y limits The data range the inset zooms into. Leave at the grayed default to auto-fit. Show zoom indicator Draws connector lines from the inset box back to the region it zooms into on the main plot.

Note: Inset axes and a broken axis are mutually exclusive — enabling one disables the other.

docs.title: Secondary Axes (Secondary & Inset Axes)
docs.text: Plot additional Y-columns (or a second X-column) against independent scales, one row per axis (Y2, Y3, X2). Each row is enabled once a column is assigned to that axis and lets you set a Label, Min/Max limits, a Log scale toggle, a Color, and a Marker.

docs.title: 4.2 Legend & Series
docs.text:
The Legend & Series category of the Customize Graph Dialog.

The Legend & Series category lets you customize the appearance and placement of the plot legend as well as per-series colors, markers, alpha, and line widths.

docs.title: Legend Box & Series Styling
docs.text:
Control Description Put legend box outside Moves the legend box to the right of the plot area, keeping it out of the way of your data. Uncheck to place it inside the plot. Unify marker size / edge color Checked by default: one Marker size / Edge color control at the top applies to every series. Uncheck to reveal per-series Marker size and Edge color columns below (for scatter/point/trendline styles), so each series can be sized/outlined independently. Label Edit the display name for each data series in the legend. Marker Choose a marker symbol for each series (available for point/scatter plots). Color Pick a color for each series from the predefined palette. Alpha / Line width Per-series transparency, and line width for styles that draw a line (line, trendline, or point with Join enabled).

Tip: The legend box can be dragged to any position directly on the plot canvas using the mouse.

Adjusting legends and colors of the selected plot.

docs.title: Legend Style
docs.text: Control Description Columns / Frame / Title / Font size / Alpha / Position Layout and appearance of the legend box itself.

docs.title: 4.3 Annotations
docs.text:
The Annotations category of the Customize Graph Dialog.

The Annotations category allows you to overlay reference lines, shapes, and text labels on top of your plot.

docs.title: Adding Annotations
docs.text:
Click one of the buttons at the top to add an annotation at the center of the current plot view:

Button Description V-Line / H-Line Adds a vertical/horizontal reference line (default: red/blue, dashed). Text Adds a text label with a rounded background box (default: yellow background). Arrow Adds a point-to-point arrow. V-Span / H-Span Adds a shaded vertical/horizontal band between two values. Box Adds a filled or outlined rectangle. Callout Adds a text label with a pointer arrow to a specific data point.

docs.title: Managing Annotations
docs.text:
All current annotations are listed below the buttons. Select an annotation to Edit or Delete it. Each annotation type's edit dialog exposes the properties relevant to it — line/span/box color, style, and width; text content, font size, color, and background; arrow/callout endpoint and pointer position.

Tip: Annotations can be dragged directly on the plot canvas. Their positions are persisted when saving the workspace. Double-clicking an annotation on the canvas also opens its edit dialog.

Adjusting the position and appearance of annotations on the selected plot.

docs.title: 4.4 General & Typography and Plot Style & Fitting
docs.text:
Typography, sorting, and style-specific options in the Customize Graph Dialog.

The General & Typography and Plot Style & Fitting categories group global typography, theme, and sorting settings alongside style-specific controls (error bars, trendlines, and histograms).

docs.title: Plot Style Options & Error Bars (Plot Style & Fitting)
docs.text:
These controls adapt to the active plot style:

Option Applicable style Description Join data points point Connects the mean values with lines between categories. Dodge overlapping points point Offsets overlapping hue groups horizontally to prevent overlap. Dodge overlapping points scatter Offsets overlapping hue groups horizontally for scatter plots. Show statistics summary wafer Overlays statistical summary (mean, std, min, max, uniformity) on the wafer map. Show error bars bar Displays error bars on top of each bar. Error bar type point, line, bar Std. Dev., Std. Error, 95% CI, or None (options depend on plot style). Cap size point, line, bar Width of the error bar end caps.

docs.title: Display, Grid & Font Sizes (General & Typography)
docs.text:
Option Applicable style Description Figure theme all styles Figure color scheme: Light or Dark. X label rotation all styles Rotates the X-axis tick labels (0–90°). Show grid lines all styles Toggles the plot's background grid lines.

Set the point size of the Title, Axis label, Tick label, and Colorbar independently (defaults: 12/12/9/10). The Colorbar size controls the tick-label text on wafer/2Dmap colorbars. The subtitle has no size control — it always renders 2 pt smaller than the title; its text is edited in the side panel, not here.

docs.title: Data Sorting (General & Typography)
docs.text:
Controls how categories and legend items are ordered:

Option Description Enable intelligent data sorting If checked, sorts the underlying dataset deterministically before plotting (recommended). If unchecked, the plot strictly preserves the original row order of the dataset. Sort by When sorting is enabled, choose the target axis for sorting: - Z (hue values): Sorts categories primarily by legend group (default).- X values: Sorts X-axis categories.- Y values: Sorts data ascending based on the Y metric.

Note: Disabling intelligent data sorting is useful if your dataset is already pre-sorted and you wish to explicitly maintain that sequence. When you change sorting settings, the legend colors are automatically reset to the default palette sequence to ensure a clean positional color scheme.

docs.title: Trendline Settings (Plot Style & Fitting)
docs.text:
Visible only when the plot style is trendline:

Option Description Polynomial order Set the degree of the polynomial fit (1 = linear, 2 = quadratic, …, up to 10). Anchor point Constrain the fit to pass through a specific point. Choose Origin (0, 0) or enter a custom (X₀, Y₀). Fit equation(s) Displays the computed equation and R² value for each hue group in a table. Click Copy to export as tab-separated text (paste directly into Excel).

docs.title: Histogram Settings (Plot Style & Fitting)
docs.text:
Visible only when the plot style is histogram:

Option Description Bins Number of histogram bins (2–500, default: 20). Overlay KDE curve Superimposes a smooth Kernel Density Estimate curve on the histogram. Fill style Choose Filled bars (default) or Step (outline only).

Colormap scale (wafer / 2Dmap): the color-scale normalization (Linear / Logarithmic / Centered) lives in Axes & Limits as the Z axis Scale.

docs.title: 5. Data Filtering
docs.text:
You can dynamically filter the plotted data by applying boolean logic expressions in the Filter field using the format: (column_name) (operator) (value).

Note: String values must be enclosed in double quotes ("text"). Column headers containing spaces must be enclosed in backticks (`column name`).

An example demonstrating how to apply filters to a dataset dynamically.

Filter Expression Resulting Behavior Confocal != "high" Excludes all data points where the "Confocal" column equals "high". Thickness == "1ML" or Thickness == "3ML" Includes only the data points where the "Thickness" column equals exactly "1ML" or "3ML". `Laser Power` <= 5 Includes data points where the "Laser Power" column is less than or equal to 5.

docs.title: 6. Statistical Calculations & Fitting Details
docs.text: For statistical plot styles (point, bar, box, and trendline), SPECTROview automatically calculates essential metrics and visualizes the distribution of your data.

docs.title: 6.1 Point and Bar Plots
docs.text:
• Central Value (Mean): The primary data point (the circle marker in a point plot or the top of the bar in a bar plot) represents the arithmetic mean of all Y-values for a given X-category.
  • Error Bars (95% CI): The error bars extending from the mean represent the 95% Confidence Interval of the mean. This is calculated using the Standard Error of the Mean (SEM): Error Bar = ± (1.96 × SEM) where SEM = Standard Deviation / sqrt(N).

docs.title: 6.2 Box Plot
docs.text:
The box plot natively displays the statistical distribution of the dataset based on standard five-number summaries:

  • Box Bounds (Q1 to Q3): The main body of the box spans from the first quartile (25th percentile) to the third quartile (75th percentile), known as the Interquartile Range (IQR).
